_comment: Golden set for the retrieval evaluation harness. Every question is answerable from the
committed fixture corpus (see README.md in this directory) except those marked UNANSWERABLE,
which are answerable from nothing in it and exist to measure the confidence gate.
'document' names a FixtureDocument constant; 'pages' are 1-based physical pages of THAT file,
not of the original book. Grading credits a retrieved chunk when its document matches and the
chunk COVERS an expected page — chunks record both ends of their page span as of Phase 13.
pageTolerance was 1 until Phase 13, and it was slack the old chunker made necessary: a fixed
window recorded only where it started, so a fact at the top of page N could sit in a chunk
stamped N-1 and the harness had to accept either. Accepting either also credited retrievals
that landed one page away and never held the answer. Section-shaped chunks know where they
end, so the slack is gone and 0 means what it says.
Sixty-four as of Phase 17, and the four new ones carry 'addedIn': 17 for a reason. Adding a
question changes the denominator of every average, so a set that grew would silently make this
phase's numbers incomparable with the ones Phases 12 to 16 published. The marker lets the
report print the headline twice: over the original sixty, which is what those phases measured,
and over all sixty-four, which is what this corpus can now be asked. V01 to V04 are questions
whose answer is in a drawing and in no sentence anywhere near it, which is the case Phase 14
closed by saying no amount of generated text would reach them.
Sixty questions, not twenty. At twenty, one question is worth five points, so a real 8% gain
and pure noise are the same number — and twelve separate changes are measured against this.
Five kinds, because they fail differently. FACTUAL is a named quantity that lexical search
alone often finds. CONCEPTUAL has little vocabulary overlap with its source and leans on the
dense half. SYNTHESIS needs pages from two places at once, which is the case top-6 truncation
breaks first. FIGURE_TABLE depends on content a text-only pipeline cannot see, so it is the
baseline the visual work is judged against. UNANSWERABLE is scored only on refusal.
Each expected page was read out of the fixture PDF and traced to the theorem, lemma or figure
caption named in 'note'. If a fixture file is re-cut, these page numbers are void.

questions.question: What running time does a LinearHashTable guarantee for add, remove and find?
questions.note: Theorem 5.2 — O(1) expected time per operation

questions.question: What is the maximum occupancy a LinearHashTable allows before it resizes?
questions.note: if (2*(q+1) > t.length) resize(); // max 50% occupancy

questions.question: At what minimum occupancy does a LinearHashTable shrink its table?
questions.note: if (8*n < t.length) resize(); // min 12.5% occupancy

questions.question: In a ChainedHashTable, what is the expected length of the list at t[hash(x)]?
questions.note: Lemma 5.2 — at most n_x + 2

questions.question: What is the expected height of a skiplist containing n elements?
questions.note: Lemma 4.4 — at most log n + 2

questions.question: How many nodes does a skiplist with n elements contain in expectation, counting the sentinel?
questions.note: Lemma 4.5 — 2n + O(log n)

questions.question: What is the maximum height of a red-black tree storing n values?
questions.note: stated in the chapter opening and proved as Lemma 9.2 — at most 2 log n

questions.question: What is the maximum height of a 2-4 tree with n leaves?
questions.note: Lemma 9.1 — at most log n

questions.question: How many comparisons does merge-sort perform in the worst case?
questions.note: Theorem 11.1 — at most n log n comparisons, O(n log n) time

questions.question: What is the expected number of comparisons quicksort performs on n distinct elements?
questions.note: Theorem 11.2 — at most 2n ln n + O(n)

questions.question: How many comparisons does heap-sort perform?
questions.note: Theorem 11.4 — at most 2n log n + O(n)

questions.question: What is the running time of counting sort on n integers drawn from 0 to k-1?
questions.note: Theorem 11.7 — O(n + k)

questions.question: What is the running time of radix sort on an array of n w-bit integers?
questions.note: Theorem 11.8 — O((w/d)(n + 2^d))

questions.question: What is the lower bound on the number of comparisons any deterministic comparison-based sorting algorithm must perform?
questions.note: Theorem 11.5 — at least log(n!) = n log n - O(n)

questions.question: How much space does an adjacency matrix use to represent a graph?
questions.note: Theorem 12.1 — O(n^2)

questions.question: How much space does the adjacency list representation of a graph use?
questions.note: Theorem 12.2 — O(n + m)

questions.question: What is the running time of breadth-first search on a graph stored as adjacency lists?
questions.note: Theorem 12.3 — O(n + m)

questions.question: What running time does an unbalanced binary search tree guarantee for add, remove and find?
questions.note: Theorem 6.1 — O(n) per operation

questions.question: Starting from an empty B-tree, how many splits, merges and borrows can a sequence of m additions and removals cause?
questions.note: Lemma 14.1 — at most 3m/2

questions.question: What running time does a YFastTrie achieve for its SSet operations?
questions.note: Theorem 13.3 — O(log w) expected

questions.question: What is the difference between a worst-case, an amortized and an expected running time?
questions.note: the three guarantees are defined together on one page

questions.question: Why is paying for fire insurance a good analogy for the difference between worst-case and expected cost?
questions.note: the house-and-insurance worked example

questions.question: What does big-Oh notation actually denote, and why is writing f(n) = O(g(n)) an abuse of notation?
questions.note: O(f(n)) denotes a set of functions; membership vs equality

questions.question: Why does randomly choosing which elements to promote keep a skiplist efficient?
questions.note: coin tosses and the expected height of the structure

questions.question: What goes wrong when a hash function distributes keys badly?
questions.note: good hash spreads keys so expected list length is O(1); a bad one does not

questions.question: How does a scapegoat tree decide that it has become unbalanced enough to rebuild?
questions.note: height compared against log base 3/2 of q

questions.question: Why is a binary search tree built from a random permutation likely to be balanced?
questions.note: every permutation equally likely; balanced trees arise from far more permutations

questions.question: Why might you prefer a red-black tree over a skiplist or a treap?
questions.note: worst-case bounds rather than expected ones, which rely on randomization

questions.question: Why must a correct comparison-based sorting algorithm's comparison tree have at least n! leaves?
questions.note: two permutations reaching the same leaf would be sorted identically, so one is wrong

questions.question: What is the external memory model and what does it count as the cost of an algorithm?
questions.note: blocks transferred between internal and external memory; internal computation is free

questions.question: Why do B-trees perform better in practice than their running-time bounds suggest?
questions.note: B is large, so 99% or more of the data sits in leaves and the internal nodes stay cached

questions.question: How can a graph model which university classes conflict with each other?
questions.note: an edge exists when at least one student takes both classes

questions.question: How is a complete binary tree stored in an array without any pointers?
questions.note: Eytzinger's method

questions.question: What is an external node in a binary tree and why is it useful to talk about them?
questions.note: the nil positions; a tree with n real nodes has n+1 external nodes

questions.question: How does the expected length of a search path in a treap compare with that in a skiplist?
questions.note: the treap chapter compares the two directly; Theorem 4.3 gives the skiplist bound

questions.question: Which search structures give worst-case O(log n) bounds rather than expected or amortized ones?
questions.note: the red-black opening claims worst case; Table 1.2 marks E and A on the alternatives

questions.question: Both scapegoat trees and red-black trees support add and remove — how do their time guarantees differ?
questions.note: Theorem 8.1 is amortized O(log n); Theorem 9.1 is worst-case O(log n)

questions.question: How does the analysis of quicksort reuse the analysis of random binary search trees?
questions.note: Lemma 11.1 translates Lemma 7.1 into a statement about pivot comparisons

questions.question: How does a YFastTrie combine an XFastTrie with treaps to reduce space to O(n)?
questions.note: stores O(n/w) values in the xft, the rest in treaps of expected size O(w)

questions.question: Where is the potential method of amortized analysis used, and for which structures?
questions.note: Lemma 2.2 for DualArrayDeque balance(); Lemma 3.1 for SEList spread/gather

questions.question: Why is the height of a B-tree so much smaller than that of a binary search tree holding the same keys?
questions.note: O(log_B n) against O(n) unbalanced / O(log n) balanced

questions.question: Radix sort beats the n log n sorting lower bound — why is that not a contradiction?
questions.note: the lower bound applies to comparison-based algorithms; radix sort is not one

questions.question: How does heap-sort use the same structure described in the chapter on priority queues?
questions.note: heapSort builds the implicit binary heap of Theorem 10.1 in place

questions.question: An XFastTrie relies on a USet internally — what does that dependency cost in running time?
questions.note: constant expected time per USet operation, which is what makes find O(log w) expected

questions.question: In the worked example of a ChainedHashTable, how many items are stored and how long is the table?
questions.note: Figure 5.1 caption — n = 14 and t.length = 16

questions.question: Which table summarises the running times of every SSet and priority queue implementation in the book?
questions.note: Table 1.2, spanning the two pages of the summary

questions.question: Which two functions are plotted against each other to show that a smaller growth rate eventually wins?
questions.note: Figure 1.5 — plots of 15n versus 2n log n

questions.question: Is there a diagram showing which chapters depend on which other chapters?
questions.note: Figure 1.6 — the dependency graph between chapters

questions.question: What black-height does the worked example of a red-black tree have?
questions.note: Figure 9.4 caption — black-height 3

questions.question: How many passes of counting sort does the radix sort figure use, and on how many bits?
questions.note: Figure 11.8 — w = 8-bit integers, 4 passes

questions.question: Which figure shows a graph next to its adjacency matrix?
questions.note: Figure 12.2

questions.question: How many vertices does the example graph used throughout the chapter have?
questions.note: Figure 12.1 caption — a graph with twelve vertices

questions.question: How many lists are stacked on top of each other in the drawing of a skiplist?
questions.note: Figure 4.1, captioned only 'A skiplist containing seven elements'. The height is in the picture and in no sentence of the chapter

questions.question: Two search trees are drawn side by side holding exactly the same keys. How do their shapes differ?
questions.note: Figure 7.1, two binary search trees over 0..14. The caption names the keys and says nothing about the shapes, which are the whole point of drawing both

questions.question: In the picture that lays a complete binary tree out as a flat array, where do a node's two children end up?
questions.note: Figure 10.1, Eytzinger's method. A student who has seen the diagram and not the formula asks it this way

questions.question: Which diagram shows the three situations that can come up when something is inserted into the middle of a space-efficient list?
questions.note: Figure 3.4, the three cases of an SEList addition. Shares almost no vocabulary with its caption, which is how a student who remembers the picture would ask

questions.question: What is the amortized running time of the union-find disjoint set structure with path compression?
questions.note: union-find is not covered anywhere in this book

questions.question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm compute single-source shortest paths?
questions.note: the graph chapter covers only representations, BFS and DFS

questions.question: What is the running time of Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm?
questions.note: spanning forests appear in an exercise; Kruskal's algorithm does not

questions.question: How does a Bloom filter test set membership, and what is its false positive rate?
questions.note: not in this book

questions.question: What is the master theorem for solving divide-and-conquer recurrences?
questions.note: recurrences are solved directly here; the master theorem is never stated

questions.question: How does a suffix tree support substring search in linear time?
questions.note: not in this book

questions.question: What is the worst-case running time of Timsort?
questions.note: not in this book

questions.note: the hardest refusal: the book covers binary tries over integers at length, so retrieval will return confident-looking trie chunks that cannot answer this
